query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A controlled heat‐treatment regimen (i.e., annealing with tailored temperature–time profiles and cooling rates) can direct the phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high‐entropy alloys by modulating the diffusional kinetics between competing FCC and BCC phases.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or homogenized Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with a mixed, non-equilibrium microstructure containing precursor FCC and/or BCC regions.
generation.intervention: Apply a systematic heat treatment procedure involving solution treatment, controlled annealing at selected temperatures for prescribed durations, followed by defined quenching/cooling.
generation.conditions: Experiments are performed under varied annealing temperatures and times, together with controlled cooling rates that allow significant but limited atomic diffusion.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase interfaces and the evolving precipitate/matrix morphology between FCC and BCC regions.
generation.mechanism: The intervention alters the diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic driving forces, thereby favoring nucleation and growth of one phase (or refining the phase mixture) over another. This temperature-time-cooling interplay shifts the free energy balance between the FCC and BCC phases, thus controlling phase fractions and microstructural characteristics.
generation.predicted_outcome: A systematic variation in the phase fractions (and potentially the associated grain/precipitate sizes) in the HEA, leading to improved or tailored mechanical properties relative to the baseline, non-optimized heat treatment condition.
generation.baseline: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs produced by conventional melting or powder metallurgy without an optimized heat treatment, resulting in a less-controlled, possibly heterogeneous microstructure.
generation.boundary: The efficacy of the heat treatment is limited to regimes where diffusion is active enough to cause phase transformations but not so aggressive that undesirable coarsening or over-aging occurs. Outside these conditions, phase control may not be achieved.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative changes in phase fractions and the optimal set of heat treatment parameters remain to be fully defined and may depend on subtle alloying and processing nuances.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples under identical casting/homogenization conditions. Subject them to different heat treatment regimes, systematically varying annealing temperatures, durations, and cooling rates. Use X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify the phase fractions and microstructural features.
measurements: Phase fraction determination via XRD and microstructural imaging
Grain and precipitate size distribution via SEM/TEM
Mechanical properties (e.g., hardness, tensile strength) correlating with microstructure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if variations in the annealing temperature–time profiles and cooling rates do not yield systematic and reproducible differences in the phase fractions and corresponding microstructural features, or if the expected correlations with mechanical properties are not observed.
